extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for evaluating inductive and syllogistic reasoning: how to form, state, test, and chain inductions and how to use syllogistic/deductive form as a test for validity. Includes warnings about habit, recording generalizations, and the limits of formal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the general theorem in its broadest form
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This theorem it is extremely important to ascertain and declare, in its broadest form of generality; and thus to place before our minds, in its full extent, the whole of what our evidence must prove if it proves any thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing an induction at maximal generality shows the full extent of what the evidence must establish; doing so focuses attention on whether the available experience suffices to support the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test generalizations by seeking contradictory known facts (reductio)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the general inference would comprise within it some fact or facts the reverse of which we already know to be true, we shall discover the error in our generalization by a reductio ad impossibile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposed general proposition implies known false consequences, that indicates insufficiency of the premises; use this as a practical test for defective generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascend to a general proposition to evaluate analogical inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In reasoning from a number of known cases to another case supposed to be analogous, it is always possible, and generally advantageous, to divert our argument into the circuitous channel of an induction from those known cases to a general proposition, and a subsequent application of that general proposition to the unknown case.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than relying on single parallels, recast analogical arguments as induction→generalization→application to expose hidden assumptions and all parallel cases at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent doubtful reasoning as induction followed by deduction (syllogistic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'An induction from particulars to generals, followed by a syllogistic process from those generals to other particulars,... is a form in which we may always state our reasonings if we please... indispensable to throw our reasoning, when there is any doubt of its validity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When validity is in doubt, state the argument as (1) the induction that yields the general rule and (2) the deduction applying that rule to the new case; this form aids detection of inconclusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require majors (general propositions) to be true in their whole extent for the argument to be maintainable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Majors ... will be general propositions embracing whole classes of cases; every one of which propositions must be true in all its extent, if the argument is maintainable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general premise used as a major must be supportable for the entire class it covers; any exception within that extent undermines the inferential chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the minor premise as affirmation of resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The minor premise always affirms a resemblance between a new case and some cases previously known... the minor... corresponds to an indispensable part of the argument itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The minor (that the subject resembles known instances in relevant respects) must be justified—by direct observation, evidence, or by a prior induction—otherwise the deduction is unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the two-part process: ascertain marks (induction) and identify them (deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'First, that of ascertaining what attributes are marks of [the property]; and, secondly, whether any given individuals possess those marks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate discovery of diagnostic marks (induction/generalization) from the application of those marks to individuals (deduction); this clarifies where evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syllogism/formal logic to secure consistency, not to establish truth
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The end aimed at by Formal Logic... is not truth, but consistency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal logical form as a tool to check consistency of statements and inferences; do not mistake formal validity for empirical adequacy—truth requires proper empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of consecrating insufficient inferences into hardened maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Inferences originally made on insufficient evidence become consecrated, and, as it were, hardened into general maxims; and the mind cleaves to them from habit... having forgotten the particulars, it does not think of revising its own former decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly re-examine entrenched generalizations against original observations and new evidence to avoid perpetuating past errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the major premise is an affirmation of sufficiency but separate the testing act from the original induction
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I quite admit that the major is an affirmation of the sufficiency of the evidence... But I can not concede that this recognition of the sufficiency of the evidence ... is a part of the induction itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish forming an induction from later reflexive verification that the evidence was sufficient; testing or stating sufficiency is a separate retrospective operation and not the induction itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using trains of reasoning, ensure each intermediate induction is grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (arsenic, governments) show conclusions may require multiple chained inductions; each intermediate generalization or resemblance must itself be supported by appropriate observations or testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex chains, trace back each link to its evidence: a minor used in one syllogism may be the conclusion of a prior induction and must be tested accordingly to avoid propagating error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record general propositions once established for future application
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The inductions may be made once for all: a single careful interrogation of experience may suffice, and the result may be registered in the form of a general proposition, which is committed to memory or to writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document well-supported generalizations to avoid redoing the evidence each time; but retain the habit of re-evaluating them when new evidence appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: A general conclusion is not the source of validity for a particular inference
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The general conclusion is never legitimate, unless the particular one would be so too; and in no sense... can the particular conclusion be said to be drawn from the general one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate particular-case inferences on their own evidential basis; the universal statement is a convenient formula for repeated application, not the ontological ground of the particular's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalize reasoning as a means of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: 'We do not need them to enable us to reason, but to enable us to know whether we reason correctly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal schemes (syllogistic expression, general propositions) not because they are the only way to think, but because they enable explicit checking and verification of inferential correctness.
